rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the full elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. An intermediate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Shorten only the gradient to test which critical pairs respond to slope while bringing the last peak closer to the 10-minute target. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed makes this a clean comparison with the scouting run.

Test a substantial temperature increase at the same gradient to probe selectivity in the unresolved clusters, especially the late triplet. Reduced retention may also create room for a shallower gradient without exceeding 10 minutes.

Use the retention-time headroom at 60 C to test a shallower gradient, with the last peak expected near 10 minutes. This isolates the slope response of the remaining early pair and late cluster at the more promising temperature.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to remove low-organic time while making the gradient slightly shallower. This may improve the remaining slope-sensitive pairs and bring the last peak below 10 minutes; the early peaks will be checked for compression.

Test whether a higher starting fraction moves the early pairs beyond their apparent selectivity crossings while improving late-pair resolution through a shallower slope. This is an exploratory step; monitor the first peaks for excessive compression.

Spend the available time headroom on a shallower gradient, targeting a last peak near 10 minutes. Holding the starting fraction and temperature fixed will reveal whether the unresolved early cluster improves along with the late pair.

Probe the opposite temperature limit to test whether selectivity can rescue the nearly slope-insensitive early pair. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature effects and reveals whether the late cluster separates on the other side of its order crossing.

Combine a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to improve the late pair while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes. This also tests whether the early cluster separates farther from its crossing, although compression of the first three peaks is a risk.

Test the intermediate starting fraction to balance early-cluster selectivity against late-pair resolution. This brackets the promising 0.20-start method while retaining a shallow gradient and a last peak expected close to 10 minutes.

Explore the steeper-gradient side of the late-cluster crossing at low temperature, where the early cluster showed better selectivity. This sacrifices some slope-dependent resolution but removes the time penalty and may separate the late peaks in a different order.

Refine the best method with a slightly shallower gradient by lowering the endpoint one grid step. This should improve the late critical pair and bring the middle pair above 1.5, with the last peak expected close to 10 minutes.

Test an earlier transition to the final hold, using a gradient slope close to the successful low-start methods. The hold may change late-pair selectivity independently of the early separation, though it risks a longer last-peak retention time.

Test intermediate temperature at the 0.15 starting fraction to shift the early cluster away from its high-temperature crossing. The shorter gradient should avoid a time penalty while assessing whether this selectivity region merits refinement.

Lower temperature one step from the best method to test whether improved early-cluster selectivity outweighs any loss in the late pair. The current retention-time margin should largely absorb the small increase in retention.

Choose a slope between injections 7 and 12 to approach 10 minutes without a time penalty. The endpoint remains above the observed elution window, so this should preserve gradient elution while improving the late critical pair over injection 7.

Refine the current best slope from 0.0458 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute, targeting a last peak just under 10 minutes. The slightly shallower gradient should improve the late pair and bring the middle pair to approximately baseline resolution.

Test a nearby selectivity balance with a lower starting fraction and a modest temperature reduction. The slope is chosen to keep the last peak near 10 minutes while potentially improving the early cluster and first-pair separation relative to the 60 C run.

Refine the alternative low-start optimum with a slope just steeper than injection 4, aiming to remove its time penalty while retaining most of its resolution. This tests whether that selectivity pattern can outperform the current best high-start method.

Test whether moving farther beyond the early-pair temperature crossing recovers more resolution than it loses in the late cluster. The steeper gradient compensates for lower temperature, targeting a last peak near 10 minutes.

Test a faster gradient followed by a lower-organic hold to change late-cluster selectivity rather than merely fine-tuning slope. The low starting fraction protects early retention, while 60 C limits the risk of excessive hold-phase retention.

Raise temperature one step from injection 18 to improve the late critical pair while retaining a penalty-free run. This directly tests whether the intermediate starting fraction offers a better overall resolution balance at the highest temperature.

Test whether moderate cooling improves the compressed early and middle pairs at the higher starting fraction. Shortening the gradient relative to injection 9 should offset increased retention, while the late cluster remains the main selectivity risk.

Make injection 23’s gradient slightly shallower to spend its remaining time margin on the unresolved middle and late pairs. The last peak is expected just under 10 minutes, potentially improving the CRF without adding a time penalty.

Use a modest temperature increase and slightly shallower slope than injection 24 to improve the late critical pair while targeting a last peak near 10 minutes. This final test balances that potential gain against temperature-driven losses in the early cluster.
